content.comment_body: Hello, I haven't worked with [product_name] yet and I'm interested to know if it can achieve what I need. Suppose I have 10 [product_name] basic modules and 10 [product_name] operator devices, each numbered for simplicity. Using Ethernet, is it possible to connect them so that each basic module communicates with its neighbors and corresponding operator device? The modules will send and receive analog signals to/from each other and their respective operator device. The modules and operator devices will be located in separate clusters about 20 meters apart. Is such a setup possible, and what Ethernet cabling layout would be recommended?

Operator devices come with a built-in two-port switch, so daisy-chaining them is feasible. The base modules can be interconnected, for example using a compact switch or a similar networking device. Each device needs a unique IP address for proper addressing.
Thank you for the information, [user_name]. I recall reading that there is a limitation of linking only nine operator devices together. Can you confirm if that's correct?

I'm not aware of that specific limitation, but you could always install two Ethernet cables between the base module area and the operator device area. The old Ethernet 5-4-3 rule isn't a concern here, but having a backup cable is a smart idea. Running two cables through walls is nearly the same effort as one, and having redundancy could be valuable in the future.

Hello [user_name], You can connect two [product_name] units with an operator device (since it has two ports) without needing a compact switch, by creating a separate program for each [product_name] and using network inputs and outputs. Is any specific configuration required for the [product_name] and the operator device?

Hi, An operator device can only communicate with one [product_name] at a time. Within the operator device, there is a list of [product_name] IP addresses, and you can select which [product_name] it communicates with. The number of devices you can connect depends on your network setup—typically, a class C network is used, with IP addresses in the 192.168.0.xxx range, allowing up to 256 devices. For your scenario, you can connect 10 base modules and 10 operator devices. Keep in mind that a [product_name] can only communicate with up to eight additional devices, one operator device, plus a PC for programming. Hope this clarifies things.

analysis.insight_summary: Users are discussing the possibilities and limitations of networking multiple [product_name] basic modules and operator devices over Ethernet. Major concerns include understanding device interconnection limits, IP address assignment, specific communication constraints (like operator devices being able to talk to only one module at a time), and cabling best practices. There is some uncertainty about maximum device counts, supported network arrangements, and the easiest, most reliable setup.
analysis.user_expectations: Users want to reliably connect several [product_name] modules and operator devices via Ethernet with clear, scalable, and robust network configuration, without encountering ambiguous technical restrictions. They expect straightforward installation, reliable data exchange, and flexibility for future expansion.
